May. The hospital has offered Mihai a permanent contract in Bucharest. The same week, a hospital in Madrid has offered him a job. In the evening, after Rosa Elena falls asleep, Ana and Mihai sit in the garden next to the little walnut tree.
We have to decide this week. The Madrid hospital wants an answer by Friday.
I know. I’ve been thinking about it for days. If you’d asked me two years ago, I’d have told you we should go back to Madrid without a second thought.
Now I’m not so sure. On the one hand, my mother is in Madrid, getting older, and so are my lifelong friends. On the other hand, here I have my job at the Cervantes, my students, the club…
And there’s my mum, with her diabetes. And Grandpa Gheorghe, who’s ninety-four. It’s not that I don’t want to go back to Madrid, Ana. But if we left now, I’d feel I was abandoning them.
I understand. And Rosa Elena? Here she goes to nursery, she speaks Romanian with her granny, she has her friends from the park…
And her walnut tree. Don’t laugh, but yesterday she asked me if the tree would come with us if we moved.
(laughs and her eyes fill with tears at the same time) And what did you tell her?
That trees don’t move. That they put down roots. And she said: “Well, so do I”.
Mihai… I think she’s already made the decision for us.
Are you sure? I don’t want you to stay for me. I want you to stay because it’s what you want.
I’m sure. But on one condition. We spend every summer in Madrid, with my mum. And you finally learn to make a proper potato tortilla.
Deal. Although the tortilla part will be the hardest.

«Por un lado… [rising tone, pause] por otro… [falling tone]». The first argument stays “hanging”, the second closes the idea.
Speak slowly and clearly; a short pause is better than filling it with “errr”. Useful expressions for buying time: «Pues…», «A ver…», «Déjeme pensar…».
eh-CHAR-ra-EE-ses: the initial “r” of raíces is rolled, and “aí” is two syllables because of the accent.

Prueba de comprensión de lectura (modelo DELE B1)
A text like the ones in the exam. Read it and answer the questions.
More and more young Europeans are deciding to live in a country other than their own. According to a recent study, one in five university students has spent at least six months abroad.

Most say the experience changed their lives. “At first I missed everything: the food, my family, the language,” admits Laura, an engineer from Seville who lives in Gdańsk. “But after a year I realised I was no longer a foreigner.”
However, it isn’t all advantages. Many point out that it’s hard to keep up friendships at a distance and that, when they return home, they feel like foreigners in their own country too.

Experts recommend that, before leaving, young people learn at least the basics of the local language. “It’s not that it’s essential,” explains a psychologist, “but it makes integration enormously easier.”

The DELE B1 exam took place on a Saturday in May, at the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest. Ana wasn’t on the examining board, because three of her students were sitting it and it wouldn’t have been fair. But she came at eight in the morning, an hour before everyone else, with a flask of coffee and a bag of croissants.

The three students were Costel, Mr Dan and a young woman from her Thursday group. Mrs Ecaterina wasn’t sitting it. “At my age,” she had said, “I set the exams.” But she came too, with a bunch of lilac from her garden, “for luck”.
Costel was the first of the three to arrive. He was wearing an ironed white shirt, a tie he clearly hadn’t worn in years, and the little red toy lorry in his jacket pocket. He was pale.
“Miss, I didn’t sleep a wink,” he said. “Last night I dreamed they asked me about the imperfect subjunctive and I could only answer in Hungarian.”
“Three words. That’s why it was a nightmare.”

Ana laughed and poured him a coffee. She reminded him of what she had told him a thousand times in class: read the questions before the texts, don’t get stuck on a word you don’t know, speak slowly in the oral exam and, if your mind goes blank, say “déjeme pensar” with a smile.
“And above all,” she added, “think of Álex. You’re not here for a piece of paper. You’re here for him.”
Costel touched the toy lorry in his pocket and nodded.

At nine sharp, a serious lady in glasses opened the classroom door and read out a list of names. The candidates went in silently, as if they were going to a funeral. Ana, Ecaterina and Mr Dan’s wife, who had come too, stayed in the corridor.

They were the longest four hours of Ana’s life. Longer than Rosa Elena’s birth, she thought later, and that’s even though that day had lasted fourteen hours. Every time the door opened, she jumped to her feet. Mrs Ecaterina, on the other hand, took out a García Márquez book and started reading calmly, as if she were on the beach.
“How can you be so calm?” Ana asked her.
“Because I’ve already done everything I could: I taught them not to be afraid,” the old lady answered, without looking up from her book. “The rest is up to them.”
At one o’clock, all three came out of the written paper. The young woman was smiling. Mr Dan had the face of someone who had just run a marathon. Costel didn’t say anything.
“How did it go?” Ana asked, trying not to look nervous.

“For the letter they asked me to write to a friend about a trip,” Costel said very slowly. “I wrote to Álex. I told him about the drive to Valencia. The thing with the lorry. The thing with ‘te iubesc’. I think I went over the word count. They asked for a hundred and twenty and I wrote two hundred.”
Ana had to bite her lip so as not to cry in front of him.

The oral exam was in the afternoon. Costel got the last slot, at five. For the monologue, he had to speak for three minutes about “an important person in your life”. Ana only found out weeks later, when one of the examiners, a young teacher from Salamanca, told her about it in the institute café.

Costel had started by talking about his grandson. He got three verbs wrong in the first minute. His mind went blank once and he said “déjeme pensar” with such a big smile that the two examiners laughed. Then, little by little, he began to talk about another person: a teacher who hadn’t let him give up, a club where a lorry driver, an eighty-year-old translator and a father who didn’t know how to talk to his son had learned together to say the important things in another language.
“He spoke for four and a half minutes,” the examiner told Ana. “We had to interrupt him. And don’t tell anyone, but my colleague had to step out for a moment to find a tissue.”

The results came a month later, in mid-June, by email. Costel was in Germany, at a motorway service station near Munich, when his phone rang. He called Ana from the cab of his lorry. At first, Ana couldn’t understand anything, because Costel was shouting in a mix of Romanian, Spanish and something that sounded like German.
“Apto!” she finally managed to make out. “It says ‘apto’, Miss! I passed! Thirty-eight in the written and forty-one in the oral!”

All three had passed. Mr Dan, by the skin of his teeth, and he celebrated as if he’d won the lottery. The Thursday girl, with a very high mark. And Costel, the fifty-eight-year-old lorry driver who had been on the point of giving up on everything, with a higher oral mark than anyone in his group.

To celebrate, the club threw a party in Ana and Mihai’s garden on the last Saturday in June. Everyone came. Costel came with his daughter, his son-in-law Vicent and Álex, who had come specially from Valencia. Andrei brought Ion Mărgărit’s Leica and took photos of everyone. Viorica came by taxi, phone in hand, and streamed the party live for her “followers”, who now numbered more than a hundred thousand.

Elena made sarmale for forty people and a sugar-free cozonac that vanished in ten minutes. Grandpa Gheorghe couldn’t come, because he no longer travelled, but he sent a bottle of țuică from his village and a voice message that Mihai played on the speaker: “Congratulations to the students. And nobody get drunk, because the țuică is strong”.

Álex and Rosa Elena spent the whole afternoon under the little walnut tree, which now had twelve leaves, playing with the red toy lorry and chatting in a mix of Spanish, Romanian and Valencian that nobody else could understand any more.
At sunset, as the sun began to sink behind the roof, Mihai tapped a glass with a fork. Everyone fell silent. Viorica raised her phone so her followers wouldn’t miss a thing.

“Ana and I wanted to take advantage of you all being here to tell you something,” said Mihai, taking Ana’s hand. “We came to Bucharest for two years, and I’ve already extended my contract once. We thought that when my contract ended, we’d go back to Madrid. This week I signed a new contract with the hospital. A permanent one.”

There was a second of silence. Then Elena dropped the cozonac tray, which luckily was already empty, and burst into tears. Costel let out a shout. Mrs Ecaterina closed her book and smiled like someone who had known this for a long time.
“We’re staying,” said Ana, in Romanian and then in Spanish, so everyone would understand. “Rămânem. Nos quedamos. Although every summer we’re going to Madrid, and anyone who wants to can come.”

Later, when almost everyone had left, Ana sat alone for a moment on the old stump, next to the little walnut tree. Rosa Elena was asleep on the living-room sofa, cuddled up with Álex and the red lorry. From the kitchen came Elena’s voice, teaching Vicent to make sarmale, and Mihai’s laughter as he tried, without success, to translate the word “varză” (cabbage) into Valencian.

Ana thought about everything that had happened since they came. The box under the floor. Vasile’s ring and Ileana’s letter. Grandpa Gheorghe and Ion, the friend who had left without saying goodbye. Yuki under the red umbrella. The thousandth crane, buried under her feet. Costel, with his tie and his toy lorry. All the words she had taught and all the ones she had learned.

She thought that if someone had told her all this on the day she arrived in Bucharest, she wouldn’t have believed it. And she also thought that, in the end, this was the most beautiful thing about learning a language: you never know where it will take you.

A walnut leaf stirred in the night breeze. Ana touched it with her fingertips, gently, like someone greeting a new arrival. And very softly, so that only the tree could hear, she said in the two languages of her home:

“soltó un grito” = let out a shout

Dear Lucía: how are things in Madrid? I’m writing to give you some news: I’ve decided to change jobs!
I’d been thinking about it for months. Although they paid me well, I wasn’t happy. If they’d offered me more free time, maybe I’d have stayed.
On the one hand, living abroad opens your mind; on the other, it’s hard to be far from your family.
In the end, it’s not that one country is better than another; the important thing is to be with the people you love.
DELE B1 mock exam: the oral exam
Prepare for 15 minutes, then speak out loud (record yourself if you can).
Task 1 (monologue, 2–3 minutes): “An important person in my life”, like Costel. Use the past tenses.
Task 2 (photo, 2–3 minutes): describe a family photo: who it is, what they’re doing, what you think happened before (guesses: estarán…, habrán…).
Task 3 (conversation): discuss with someone (or with yourself) the topic: ¿Te gustaría vivir en otro país? ¿Por qué? ¿Qué echarías de menos?
Task 4 (situation): you’re at a hotel reception and your room isn’t the one you booked. Solve the problem politely (conditional, subjunctive: me gustaría que…).
Congratulations: you’ve finished the B1 level! Briefly reread stories 37–66 and notice how much you understand now.
